items.body: The Estonian diatonic accordion (lõõtspill) has four rows of keys and can play only in major. Tarmo Noormaa studied it for five years at the University of Tartu Viljandi Culture Academy, then spent an exchange year at the Sibelius Academy in Helsinki, where the Finnish accordion virtuoso Antti Paalanen was one of his teachers, alongside the Norwegian player Tom Willy Rustad. The instrument is native to one specific corner of the Baltic, a tradition entirely its own. Estonia built its modern cultural identity the same way: a country of one and a half million that spent fifty years under Soviet occupation and came back to itself in 1991 by going back to what was specifically its own. The instrument is also the reason a 24-year-old was handed the programming of Viljandi Folk Music Festival in 2006, and the reason he is still there now, twenty years on, with the 33rd edition due to run from 23 to 26 July. The route to that role was a roundabout one. Noormaa came to music late, and almost studied philosophy instead, as he put it when we spoke by phone in late April, a little more than three months before the festival opens, with his curated line-up days old and just shared to the world. “I started playing music in my teens, late teens only. Before that, I was not so interested. I started because of my friends and the community I had in high school. That’s when I became interested and started playing, and understood that I didn’t want to do anything else, just play music. Then I went to university to study philosophy. But I thought, no, it’s not for me, it’s a waste of time. I need to study music!” So he did, in the Folk Music Department at the Viljandi Culture Academy. The academy sits at the centre of Estonia’s largest annual music festival, one of the biggest folk gatherings in northern Europe, and Noormaa first came to it as a teenage attendee, not a programmer. “First time I participated, I think I was 17 or 18. Back then I didn’t know much about folk music or anything. I remember climbing over the fence with my friends to get in, because I didn’t want to pay money for the ticket. A few years later, I was the Programme Head of the festival.” The team had spotted him as a driven student who already organised masterclasses inside the Academy, and they brought him on to run it. The prospect was daunting. “I felt like my leg was shaking, let’s say.” He learned with the team behind him. “They helped me a lot in this process.” The legs have long since stopped shaking, and twenty years into the role, the process is entirely his own. Noormaa builds each edition in layers. A theme is set first, then a description of what that theme means musically. A national call for ideas opens in August. Around sixty or seventy proposals come in from Estonian performers, and roughly twenty to thirty are picked. After that, Noormaa approaches the artists he wants beyond the open call, and starts the conversation about whether they can do something extraordinary in Viljandi. Commissions are part of this layer. “Most Estonian folk music artists want to perform at the Viljandi Folk Music Festival, because this is their home festival. This is where they meet the core audience, where they launch their albums and present new projects, because this is where they get the most attention.” The trust that comes with that runs both ways. “I feel special about it, that they put us in this place and they want to come out. But it is also a great responsibility to present their music in the best way possible.” He brings the same attention to the international programme, travelling to festivals abroad and bringing favourites back. The festival grew out of the Estonian national revival of the early 1990s, the same period that restored independence. The question of what it meant to be Estonian after fifty years of Soviet occupation ran through everything, and folk music carried some of the weight of the answer. “It came with the idea of creating some special musical expression that is based on roots, but it is relevant nowadays, it lives nowadays. It’s not a copy of history, it’s not a museum. It’s not even a genre for us, not a musical genre. It’s the way how we experience the world.” It is a definition wide enough to contain almost anything, and the programme reflects that. For Estonian artists, the bar is the link to historical tradition. They can work from archival material, play revived folk instruments, or build crossover projects, but the core must hold. “Basically, when we listen to the music, we want to understand where this band is from, based on the sound. When you eat food, we want the staple to be folk music and all the additions can be whatever. The staple have to be very clearly folk music.” While, for foreign artists, the bar is different and stricter. They must be representative of their culture or virtuoso players within it, and they must be culturally significant at home. “People from that country or region tell you: this is the band you should invite. This is the band we want to invite to our wedding. Then we bring them here, and it is a good comparison point.” A booking, however, can always go wrong. When Noormaa has seen the act himself, or a colleague he trusts has, the call is clear. Otherwise he goes on what he can find, a YouTube clip, whatever the band sends over. “But I haven’t seen them live. So then it’s a risk.” That has happened a couple of times. Once, an act vetted off its album turned up as a different band entirely. “One band, on their album, they were very nice. They played their traditional music, but when they came to the concert, it seemed they had released another album in the meantime. They did covers of rock music. They said, oh, didn’t you know, this is our latest music?” The artists who understand what Viljandi is and stands for don’t just turn up and play. Most stay three or four days, giving workshops, jamming in the castle grounds, playing for dancing until four in the morning, sitting on the grass with audience members between sets. “It’s very important for us that they are not only great musicians, but they are also open to communicate and create interpersonal relationships.” Most of the time it works. “Usually we ask them to give a workshop. Then you already understand if they are ready to give one, which means they are ready to share. Some artists are not ready, but they are still great. So we compromise on that. But most of our artists, we want them to be able to create contact with the audience. They have to be great communicators. They have to create a participatory space, whether through dancing, singing, storytelling, or somehow engaging.” The festival’s own purpose sits underneath this. “The goal is not just to organise the festival. The festival is a tool to achieve a certain goal. It is the best tool to influence people to like folk music. We think that folk music is really very good for community building. You get a sense of belonging, of identity. It fits the revival narrative of re-independence in the 90s. People were looking for identity. What shall we do? Who are we now?” Each edition turns on a theme. For 2026 it is To Each Their Own Instrument, which Noormaa frames as two questions. “This year’s topic is folk music instruments, the instrument as a means to make this music, like a tool. You can compare the cultures: the same instrument in different cultures, how does it sound. Or different instruments, how do they differ.” For a festival built on the idea that music carries cultural identity, the instrument is a natural place to look. It tells you where something comes from, who shaped it, what survives in the way it is played. It is also the lens through which Noormaa introduces this year’s line-up. When he talks about the theme, he starts with Manhu. Sani people from the Stone Forest region of Yunnan in southwest China, a subgroup of the Yi minority, playing together since 2003, their sound is built on instruments found almost nowhere else. “They come from a minority in West China, from Yunnan, and they have these very particular instruments. They have found a way to make it work, and it is all based on folk music instruments. There are a couple of Western instruments in the band, but the core is folk music instruments.” Their international debut Voices of the Sani, released on Riverboat Records in 2020, sets the gourd-pipe lusheng and the three-string adiza lute against electric bass and drum kit. He also brings up Amy Laurenson from Shetland, where the piano made its way into folk music in a way it never quite did elsewhere, used to accompany dances where on the mainland a fiddle would play. She grew up in that tradition. Her debut album Strands was longlisted for the Scottish Album of the Year Award in 2024, the year after she was named BBC Radio Scotland’s Young Traditional Musician of the Year. “She plays piano. In Estonia, we don’t have piano in folk music. Piano is usually associated with other styles of music. But in Shetland, as well as Scotland or Denmark, even this piano is in folk music and it’s played differently. It is the same instrument, but it’s played differently, and the way it’s played, I think it’s really fascinating. You can play for a dance with piano.” From Cape Verde comes Nancy Vieira, one of the leading living voices of morna, the country’s defining song form and a fixture on UNESCO’s intangible cultural heritage list since 2019. By the standard Noormaa sets for foreign artists she belongs easily, a singer who carries real cultural weight at home, and morna is a first for the festival’s programme. Part of the point is to widen what Estonian audiences hear. With Vieira, though, he reaches for a simpler reason. “She’s an amazing singer, just pure gold. You just listen and you just like it.” The comparison-point logic that shapes most of the international programme gives way here to plain pleasure. “Sometimes it’s not only about introducing your tradition. It’s also about having an aesthetic experience.” The domestic programme shows what twenty years of community-building looks like in practice. “There are many new bands coming up. You can see them in Viljandi.” Trifoor are among the newest, opening Thursday fresh from the Young Folk Band 2025 title: “young girls playing this folk rock type of music.” Nova Lyre, on Friday, have been in the community longer, a string ensemble whose academic musicians found folk music through the Ethno camps and stayed. “How they do it is really cool, how they play. They have their own sound.” He also points to Sounds and Stories from Ruhnu Island, a trio reviving the fiddle music and hymn tunes of Ruhnu, a small island in the Gulf of Riga whose Swedish-speaking community left for Sweden in 1944. The trio pairs the fiddling of Karoliina Kreintaal and Lee Taul with Kairi Leivo‘s singing and storytelling. “I think they have a very good concept and very good players there.” On Saturday, Keelepeksjad come from somewhere else entirely: jazz musicians whose grandfathers played folk music. “They remember these songs from their childhood and bring it out in their own new way. I think it’s really cool.” The longest story belongs to OOPUS, whose third album Reivlender arrived in early 2026, more than a decade after they started. “I’m very proud of them. They have put full life into this music. They deserve it. They are really, really focused, dedicated to what they are doing.” OOPUS are reaching what Noormaa calls “superstar status” in Estonia. That kind of sustained career was rare when he started. “When I started, there were a couple of bands that had this international capacity, let’s say. But they had few concerts, couldn’t sustain their careers, and split up. What we have done over the years is we have tried to make this ecosystem of artist creation.” It begins with baby workshops. It runs through folk music competitions, three age-graded Ethno camps with the oldest going up to 29, a biennial band competition with mentoring on technical riders, marketing and stage positioning, and the festival itself as the proving ground. “All these musicians performing abroad in showcase festivals have come from that ecosystem through the Ethno experience, through the competitions.” At the camps they meet others from home and abroad, form bands, and earn slots across the calendar, learning as they go. The ones who break through return as mentors, Maarja Nuut among them, sharing what they learned. The pie is visibly bigger than it was. Over his twenty years the audience has changed in two ways, both of which bear out the approach. “People are more music focused nowadays, really enjoy the music. Before it was more about party and people drinking and not ending up in the concerts so much.” The shift shows the moment a set begins. “When the concert starts, the food area is empty. Everybody’s in front of the stage.” They are also readier to take part. “People are very engaged. They want to dance, they want to sing, they are pretty much ready to learn.” The second change is age: the share of teenagers, roughly 15 to 22, has grown alongside the festival’s long-standing family crowd. “They are full of energy. When you have a concert and young people start to party, they make the concert a party.” All of it runs on a year-round institution. Around 15 permanent staff run the Estonian Traditional Music Center from a renovated granary in Viljandi Castle Hills, with a venue, a library, and concert and educational programmes through the year, and the festival is about half its work. Across the four days the team grows to roughly 400, including 250 volunteers and outside firms for security and stage production, and the weekend draws around 27,000 visits, with 10,000 to 12,000 people a day. How much further it should grow is the open question. Noormaa and his team are drawing up a strategy for 2027 to 2029, and the first decision is whether to expand at all. He points to the Korrö Folkmusic Festival in Sweden. “They have decided that they don’t want to grow. They want to preserve how they are, because if they grow, they have to compromise on something. And then it’s not the same festival again.” Viljandi has held within about five per cent for years, and he is content to hold there. “We would like it to be bigger. But in order to make it bigger, we have to fulfil the space right now, then we can grow. We haven’t been able to fulfil the current space fully.” What the festival is ultimately for sits underneath that caution, and the answer runs deeper than size. Noormaa is now doing a master’s on his own tradition, the diatonic accordion, asking why people take it up. “The main motivation is the sense of belonging: they want to belong to the cool group that plays this music. Folk music is open to anybody. Whatever instrument you play, whatever level you play at, you will find your place in our community.” He came up the same way, and the welcome is what held him. “I felt very welcomed, very appreciated. Whatever I did, I got a lot of acknowledgement. It kept me going.” The players following him now move faster than he did, with teachers and a community he lacked. “I was here. They stepped on me, and now they are here. When I hear that they are better than me, it makes me very proud.” That belief shapes what he tells a newcomer. He trusts the festival to make its own case. “Just show up. I tell my friends: go and see the concert, let them be open and they will impress you. They will impress you for sure. I guarantee you that. I give you a money back guarantee. That’s why there are a lot of free events. It’s not only about what happens on the stage. The festival is always about what is between the stages: the jam session, the mood, how the audience is dressed up, how they communicate, what is happening. And you will be surprised positively for sure.”   The 33rd edition of Viljandi Folk Music Festival runs from 23 to 26 July 2026 while much of it free, passes for the ticketed concerts are available through viljandifolk.ee & Sviby   The post Interview: Tarmo Noormaa: From Fence-Jumping to Booking Viljandi Folk Music Festival (June 2026) appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — Approaching an album like this, one that many people love and others ignore, an album that even the band members themselves don't consider among their favorites, should be both an intellectual and a spiritual exercise. Atom Heart Mother can be many things: an orchestral album, an acoustic album, a transition between psychedelia and progressive rock... and I think it's all of that and much more. It's a dreamlike experience, with the sounds of carts and horses, grain falling into bowls and dripping taps... it's choirs and trumpets and strings... it's the greenest, greenest countryside imaginable (because it rains often in England) and it's London bathed in neon lights... it's one of my favorite Pink Floyd albums.They weren't alone; behind the nearly 24-minute main suite was Ron Geesin, who in turn drew inspiration from the French composer Edgar Var�se. The atonal trumpets are present from the very beginning, and the magic unfolds like a magic carpet beneath our feet, carrying us away, because the music includes us. Nick Mason's drums are at the forefront throughout the album; there's something dramatic, even epic, reminiscent of Spaghetti Westerns and Ennio Morricone, while at the same time never ceasing to be typically British.The orchestral ensemble, with its strings, winds, and rock band, was the most successful to date, primarily because it allowed them to maintain Pink Floyd's signature spirit of jazzy, improvised psychedelia, while simultaneously showcasing Richard Wright's classical piano skills. Furthermore, the dramatic tenor of the work was intelligently sustained, carefully paced in sections. When the guitar faded, the keyboard would enter... followed by the soprano... and then the entire choir, ensuring that we never lost the distinct feeling of listening to Pink Floyd.The choir leaves...returns...sometimes harmonious, sometimes dissonant, until the tenors join the sopranos; we're literally walking on clouds, or is it the mist of the countryside? And when the entire choir is presented in full force...the drums join in again with those touches that can only be classic-symphonic; the choir barks, Frank Zappa's sense of the absurd also present. The Hammond organ plays funk, and Gilmour joins in.And improvising with the choir, and the trio of organ, drums and bass, at least in the instance of composing the work together, was very daring on their part, when the orchestra attacks and then withdraws...a section of electronic music that reminded me of the experiments of Spooky Tooth & Pierre Henry on the album Ceremony, a matter that they would later delve deeper into on their next album.Towards the end, as if seeing the entire journey in a single second, we hear everything together in a chaotic mass of sound... ordered by the orchestra, deeper and more profound than ever. The violin remains alone with us, and time seems to stop. Doesn't the keyboard, now accelerating, mark the time? Or is it sand falling through an old clock?The guitar appears to turn at a 90-degree angle, and the choir returns with the drums blasting from all sides, hinting at a retreat... only to return and make the ending even more epic, its classical and revolutionary grandeur lingering in the sky long after it has ended, like the smoke from Pink Floyd's multicolored fireworks.This was just side one, and while it was the central track, the one that gave the album its name, the record continued, and several more surprises lay ahead. It was the era of the unexpected, surprising Pink Floyd, that group of friends who had fun experimenting in the studio. "If" is an acoustic track with Waters' signature sound, later joined by Gilmour's electric guitar, and Roger sings it in a bucolic, serene, intimate style, as the band could be at this time, grandiose, bombastic, and also simple and relaxed. Rick Wright's contribution is invaluable, as his piano notes add feeling...warmth...to a Sunday atmosphere after a hectic Saturday.Summer '68 was composed and sung by Richard Wright, a strange track for Pink Floyd's repertoire...but not in this era when anything could happen...with a piano melody that unfolds peacefully until baroque trumpets burst in, and then a section with an exquisite piano piece, along with the accompanying acoustic guitar, and that playing with the piano that made the band feel close, perhaps more than they would ever be again.Fat Old Sun belongs to David Gilmour, almost mirroring the format of Ummagumma, with its individual pieces following the collaborative work. It continues the melancholy that permeates the entire album, without abandoning its simplicity. Its final guitar solo is very emotive and provides the necessary energy at this point in the record. Somehow, they managed to make each track a journey through the countryside...and through the city, very much in the London style, varying the atmospheres and moods.Alan's Psychedelic Breakfast is another kind of suite, closing the album, almost a sociological study of the famous "most important meal of the day," illustrated with exquisitely beautiful musical pieces. Pink Floyd at their best. Rise and Shine is the first section, with piano and guitar, almost classical, with Nick Mason playing brushes almost like a Claude Bolling record. That promised country atmosphere from the cover is still present; you can almost breathe it. You enjoy every sound of breakfast with Alan, which takes us back to when we first heard the album. Sunny Side Up is the second section, with acoustic guitar, and its counterpoints with the electric guitar contribute to the spirit of the relaxed atmosphere... Morning Glory is the last one, with all the instruments together while the eggs are frying...with each drop of oil that jumps the instruments hit, and the drums are everywhere again, with the piano becoming an organ, and acquiring a presence of transcendence.Often, the composers themselves lose sight of the magnitude of their work; the very proximity of its creation deprives them of perspective, the necessary distance to judge it from another angle. Atom Heart Mother shines with the revolutionary modernity it displayed at its premiere, showcasing a band with multiple facets, both experimental and deeply human.

This band was formedin Donostia-San Sebastian, Spain which is the Basque region of the country but this band didn'tfollow in the footsteps of the folk inspired acts that spanned the latter 70s to the early 80s butrather was looking towards the more international scene which offered a larger audience beyond thesmall Basque language speaking population.The band began it all with this debut MANIFESTO which wouldn't be released until 1991 but stillshowed clear influence from Marillion and other neo-proggers from the 80s. The album features fivetracks at over 46 minutes with all but one around the 8 minute run or more. The lineup featuresguitarist To�o Cruz, bassist and flautist Jose Mari Aguirrezabala, and electronic drum programmerMikel Tor�s. Eschewing both the Basque and Spanish languages, the album is entirely in English andlooks primarily towards the British lexicon for inspiration. This is what i truly call pain prog as the band has plenty of great ideas on board but marredunfortunately by rather insipid compositions, cheesy electronic drums and one of the worst vocalistsi've ever heard in a prog context. The opening "Lednevir" starts off promising with a space rockfeel but beginning with "At The Mountains Of Madness" the theatrical vocals kick in which suggests anot so ready for primetime version of Peter Gabriel clumsily fumbling throughout the track'sprocession. While the guitars and keyboards that provide an elegant atmospheric effect are all in order therather bland drumming style suggests the absolutely worst case scenario evoking some of the 80sworst neo-prog bunglers such as I.Q's abysmal "Are You Sitting Comfortably?" for example.Unfortunately nothing improves as the album goes on and by the time "The Joker" is unfolding itssprawling never-ending repetitive monotony it just starts to become a bad parody of itself. Couldthis seriously be the worst prog band ever to emerge from Spain? Well this album suggests that to bethe case.There aren't too many albums i would deem nauseating enough to award only one star but this is oneof them. The vocals are the worst offender. Imagine the lead singer of Einstũrzende Neubauten tryingto sing operatic and you might have an idea of what to expect. Likewise the companions are ratherclumsy with the instrumental interplay fairly amateurish and to top it all off the percussion isjust plain crap. I have a high tolerance for lots of music seeing things in it that most cannot orrefuse to however this one is too much for even my sensibilities to withstand. Just awful and isampled it more than once just to make sure i wasn't being too hastily disgusted!

items.body: Review by Aussie-Byrd-Brother — German band Electric Orange have been around in some form for thirty years now, founded by Dirk Jan M�ller, a multi-instrumentalist who primarily handles keyboards alongside frequent contributor Dirk Bittner. An eclectic and constantly morphing act, the group has released multiple works across a range of styles, everything from prog rock, psych, Can-modelled grooves and even trance, before eventually finding their current calling in slowly unfolding Krautrock-flavoured ambient jams. Accompanied by bassist Werner Wieczorek and returning drummer Eric Karow from their earlier `Abgelaufen' and `Fleischwerk' days, 2023's `Gap' offers four vibrant and unpredictable jams, essentially two side-long pieces and a couple of shorter intervals around them, but all together making for another superb, fully improvised modern psychedelic record.Opener `Cyanine' launches with a lurching funkiness that melts into a murky shamble of whirring machine oscillations and maddening tribal-like drums. Initially sounding like it's submerged, the eerie and cavernous fifteen minute `Merkstein' drifts with weeping guitar strands, maddening pulses and ethereal wisps. It grows in dangerous dread as it free-falls into an unhinged stormy whirlwind of thrashing drums and wildly wavering distortion, a sense of unease and disorientation completely permeating.The flip side's `Gap' is a short up-tempo and rambunctious dash of strident guitar shimmers over scorching Hammond organ bleeds that reminds of Norwegian group Elephant9. Almost sounding like a more muscular version of late 60's/early 70's `Piper/Saucerful...' era Floyd, `Das Bunte' starts as a languid jazzy shuffle of chilled-out organ that quickly turn swirling and frantic around rumbling acid guitar attacks, all building in breathless into a droning and sucking vacuum of noise - phew!While it may lack the depth and immersive heavier moods of some previous recent Electric Orange albums, `Gap' still holds plenty of colourful jams full of spontaneity with lively playing, topped off with a gorgeously lo-fi production that retains a scuzzy grit.In this instance, the `Gap' of the title is likely not thinking of this album as being a `stop-gap' in the Electric Orange discography, rather clearly referring to the spot in your brain where deranged, immersive and sh*t-hot psychedelic music lodges itself!Four stars.

items.body: Review by tszirmay — This is the 6th album by the veteran Neo-prog band from Germany, and my second, as I enjoyed 2020 album "Beyond the Rainbow". The group is now led by Derk Akkermann (guitars, keyboards), with Lutz Guenther (bass, vocals) and Jimmy Keegan (drums) taking up some of the other slots in the band. Lead vocals are provided by the powerful voice of Henrik Wager, ably assisted by that other voice-like instrument the saxophonist (Mark Arnold) . Lead guitar duties are handled by the celebrated Martin Schnella (Frequency Drift, Seven Steps to the Green Door, Schnella/Mau, Flaming Row etc?). As a rule for Neo to work well, the songs require punch, variation, detail and expert playing by all involved. Generally, the vocals play a massive role and will demand strong voices . I can immediately attest that Saris has all the tools at its disposal. The style is mostly energetic with a domineering rhythm section that engineers quite the throttle power. There is also a calculated offer of variations that alter the modulation, from sensible to bombastic, sometimes even within the same arrangement. For slight references sake, think modern day Foreigner or Uriah Heep, in places. 10 tracks 74 minutes of music : Abfahrt! Blasting off the launchpad , heading for the amazing "Off World" shows Henrik singing initially on a lower register, a very cool idea, as the choppy Keegan-led attack has the rhythmic fusillade of a Kashmir, especially when integrated with string orchestration that transmit enormous power and strength, twinkling keyboards keeping the tension alive. The magical Arnold sax raises the piece to ethereal heights, making this an excellent modern prog delight , I really enjoy when the symphonic details kick in, the inspiration becomes immediately more personal. A super strong track that may deserve your immediate attention. "Mamucium" stays on the same path with another theatrical demonstration, though I must say the previous track is still ensconced in my mind. Henrik continues to impress as he yearns 'to go home', the Akkermann keyboards doing a yeoman's job on the ivories and Keegan bashing away like only he can. Settling gently at first, "For All Mankind" slams on the turbo power, with Henrik scaling like an athletic alpinist tackling the Eiger, with Arnold given free reign to blow a mean horn. Otherwise, the track is rock solid and eminently hummable, albeit with fists pumping . "My Pocket" has some lovely moments, the guitar solo in particular, the melody with a slight Styx like feel, melodically solid but really too short to be on par with the above. But things ramp up in a colossal fashion from hereon in, starting with the consummate "Is Anybody Out There" ,where the medieval-flavoured intro on a harpsichord does a tumultuous impression, blooming into an ongoing rotund bass line that is devastatingly effective, and quite intricate, as the stately keys kick in, the piano adding loads of spice, waiting for some of the finest vocals heard in a long time, Henrik killing it big time, flush with intense conviction. In a fair world, this tune would be played on all radios, globally. Schnella slithers in like a helical serpent, scouring the turbulent skies above, as if looking for any kind of alien salvation. "Surrounded" is the lengthiest track here, clocking a lofty 12 minutes and change , proving beyond any doubt, the attention to detail and musicality they instill in their compositional methodology. Here one can witness the fine line in the sand between neo and symphonic being reduced to a mere scratch. Everything is given more room to ramble, the organ in particular is liberated from any time shackles, the sax roaming freely, the vocals soaring both massed and solo. The melodic buildup is effortless and utterly convincing, verging on brilliance, like climbing up a series of lofty terraces, each one wider and brighter. And all along the watchtower, the booming bass and drums keep the atmosphere forcefully tidy, rock solid and comprehensive. When Schnella gets his cue, he unleashes a sizzling lightning bolt of fiery fury, as if outraged for being 'encircled'. The keyboard upsurge evolves into a paroxysm of passion, atmosphere and melody that hits one right between the ears. One more trip around the compound, to nail the coffin shut. Here are two prime examples of why Neo-Prog can be deliriously entertaining! The robust rocker "The Bounty" which chugs along masterfully, ideally paced to keep the thrills and spills always on the edge. Akkermann increases his guitar skills to fit well with his first-rate keyboards, a gifted player, to say the least. Henrik does possess a terrific set of lungs and superb control as well, another ear-opener that will not subside at anytime during the set. While this was really good, the next few have blown me off my chair. "Fill Me with Emptiness" has that bombastic Heep feel, the churning organ and screeching guitar coalescing in faultless harmony, laying down the spinal chord (sic) of the piece with aplomb, verve and audacity . When Henrik clutches the microphone, fasten your seatbelts as he also supplies the higher voice interval. After the obligatory axe solo, the second lap reveals an even heavier steamroller on the Hammond, while the dual voices rise way up above the clouds, delightfully interspaced, with Henry rapping very slightly. This did not fill me with any emptiness. An 11-minute opus, "Wish It Away" shows the way through some imaginary yellow brick road, where reality is taken over by dreams, the blackboard erased and a fresh start beckons. No scarecrow, tinman or lion in Toto's way. The forceful Akkermann piano settles the sensation, using his keyboard like a percussion instrument, the spinning dervish vocals looping like a kite caught in a hurricane. Arnold applies a jazzy expanse on the arrangement, a welcome detail. Each musician expresses themselves with delirious intent, illustrated by an almost Tangerine Dream synth sequencer bit that lasted only a few seconds caught my attention. Absolutely well-crafted prog music. To prove the astuteness of this band's modus operandi, the intense symphonics are now maintained on "Time is Killing Me, I daresay maybe even enhanced as Arnold does his finest restraint on this overpowering beauty, Henrik convincing once again (as if there was any doubt LOL) and riding the melodic wave with bravado and eloquence. The tortured bass guitar does wonders down in the basement, churning like a hundred elastics, while they keys behave like an orchestra, the shivering guitars given carte blanche. The last three tracks really sealed the deal for me. The clock is ticking. 4.5 Indian robes

items.body: Review by tszirmay — Phideaux is baaaack! A consummate American songwriter, multi-instrumentalist and vocalist, he has launched a long list of staggering albums commencing in 2003 with 'Fiendish' (that should be a clue) , getting critical recognition with 2006 release 'The Great Leap' (go figure with a title like that) and sealing the deal with 2007's 'Doomsday Afternoon' which really hit the mark. Three more tasteful albums (Number Seven, Snowtorch, and Infernal, the latter appearing in 2018) and then, there was silence. Back well-rested and surely inspired, the prog community would surely be highly expectant of what may be in store. More of same, or a slight diversion? Well let me help the process. Lots of guest musicians appear to back the man on his ,at times intricate and original compositions, some returning to the fold as well as new additions, the most recognizable is Fernando Perdomo on guitars and Rich Mouser (guitars, keyboards and percussion).The style is very vocal centric (with six different voices to supply the lung power). Eight tracks, the final an epic, for a total of42 minutes of enjoyment. Introduction done! "Do What you Will" divvies up a modern electro-pop opener that could have been a Stranglers tune revisited, the instrumentation coherent and eclectic (the piano motif is intoxicating), the dejected lyrics on the other hand are dark and grim, a slight apocalyptic feel that fits the current times of interminable negativity, solved with a deliberate shrug of hopeless argument. Phideaux vocals not only shine in lead mode but also with the backing vocal department, giving this piece an organic vigor that goes very much noticed. Keeping in line with further analysis of the human condition, "Hey Humanity" reminds us that alleged evolution is just a marketing term, as outside of technology, we have really not evolved much at all. Two steps forward and three steps back. The overt chorus is a flamboyant plea that pulls at the heartstrings, crisscrossing voices blending in with the strident guitars and pushing the pain along for evermore. The sounds are tidy and efficient on "Driving to Destruction", the massed vocals remindful of some manifestation of the distraught, the jangly keys and twisted frets combine to highlight the unescapable shambles. This could have ben a proggy Sparks track, its that serious! This town isn't big enough for all of us. A semi-romantic reprieve on "Stay with Me", a reasonable ballad that has a melodic anchor that weighs heavily on the frayed nerves of depression, angst, and fear for the future. The pleading lyrics hit hard, the chorus intensely attractive, regardless of the outcome. "Don't go away, leave it all behind". Chaplin, Hebdo, Kirk ? Does it really matter who? Well, "Charlie Knew", a bouncy, deeply evocative affair, laden with lavish orchestrations and massive choir states the message of knowledge. It maintains, even elevates the momentum of the album; while leaving the meaning to one's own discretion. The stunning wailing vocal crowns the "Siren in the Storm", as if sitting comfortably on a basalt crag, surrounded by aquatic turbulence and gale-force winds, beckoning Phideaux into looking for deliverance, rescue and finality, smiling so beautifully. Violent violins slide along mercilessly on "Enigmatic Terminus", acting as a segue to the earlier "Driving to Destruction", whirling swirls of madness and confusion, all within theatrical confines, as if a soundtrack from a scene in some movie. Two excellent tracks that ideally set up the grand finale. The 14 minute + "Legend of Mary Jo" delivers a wider palette for exuberant storytelling (I do hope I get the tale right), the instrumental stage is set for the spotlight to shine on the lyrical content, when in 2062, a prophet called Amy will come for you, riding on a white stallion, but Mary Jo will defy the odds and save us all. Phideaux is no Pavarotti (very few are) but here, he hits all the crucial high notes with a languorous dedication, giving even more depth to the titanic struggle, trumpets sounding in the background. For a moment, this musically recalls the epic Gordon Lightfoot classic "the Wreck of the Edmund Fitzgerald", as it has a slight folky structure, the honky-tonk piano not withstanding. The saxophone blurts in wonderfully , at the most opportune time, adding some brassy shine to the proceedings. Then, out of the blue, the assault on the senses begins, initiated by a basalt bass undertow, slashing guitars, dense mellotronic cascades, and tectonic drumming entering the fray, as if the Wake of Poseidon was an inspiration. The final chapter is repeated from the onset, this time slower and more deliberate, as if fatigue would have kicked in. You never walk alone, as they say in Liverpool. Excellent return to the fold, now no more lengthy sabbaticals Mr Xavier, please. 4.5 android hostilities

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — 'Masters of Illusion' is one of the recent studio albums by Welsh prog band Magenta, a group frontedby ex-Cyan keyboard player and composer Rob Reed, undoubtedly an excellent musician, who forms thecore of this neo-prog project alongside vocalist Christina Booth and guitar player Chris Fry. Thesound of this album is perhaps best described as warm, cinematic, and uplifting, as this is veryclearly a well-composed symphonic prog album that bears strong resemblance to bands like Genesis,Camel, Solstice, Tiger Moth Tales, and Fish-era Marillion, among others.The six songs that appear on 'Masters of Illusion' vary in length, but there is not a single shorttrack here. In fact, this album features three absolutely melodic prog epics with graceful guitarsolos and excellent keyboards, with Rob Reed and Chris Fry laying down some marvelous segments thatrival the intensity and emotional resonance of some of the classic Genesis recordings from the 70s.Opening track 'Bela' and the title track, which closes off the album with some sixteen minutes oflush and sophisticated prog, are to my ears the major highlights on this album. The rest is reallysolid but can sometimes feel a little flat and monotonous, with the band relying a little too muchon the pastoral, symphonic-laden aesthetic. The vocals are exquisite all throughout and at timesremind me of Kate Bush, which is interesting. There are some guest appearances from Peter Jones andJohn Mitchell, but these are very subtle, and you might not recognize their contributions unless youread the album credits. Overall, I find 'Masters of Illusion' to be very enjoyable and well-produced, and I firmly believe that it is a fine album that will definitely impress fans of neo-progand symphonic art rock.

items.body: Review by alainPP — KARFAGEN, Antony KALUGIN's band, has traded the whimsical for the progressive music of the new kingdom.OMNI (Part 4): "The Glass of Time Part 1" is the instrumental track where Antony's velvety keyboards accompany John's bucolic flute and Michel's Oldfield-esque guitar for a melting melody. Rob contributes to the romantic keyboard flourishes for this solemn opening, reminiscent of either Genesis 2 or Camel. "Frozen Rivers" features Roine contributing his signature blend of sweetness and grit, while John amplifies the symphonic pastoral effect. A multi-layered track with Marek's saxophone and Roine's brother's bass creates a crescendo of pop-love songs. "Shadowbound" follows, with Maria as a guest vocalist, setting the stage ablaze, initially channeling Kate Bush and then Floor Jansen. A powerful, dramatic track where the vocals contribute to the evolution of this symphonic, dramatic, and romantic neo-prog, reminiscent of metal. "The Shape of Love," featuring Marco for the melodramatic break, is a centerpiece brimming with neo-prog, with its meandering flute and folk-like guitar. Midway through, an ethereal interlude unfolds, with Marco speaking in a solemn solo?a divine moment that reinforces the soothing crescendo, perfect.OMNI (Part 5): "Carry On" evokes the rhythmic feel of Genesis, the 80s sound. Yogi delivers a melodic, marshmallow-like pop-rock sound filled with Antony's lush synths. This crowd-pleaser is notable for its midway break, an introspective vocal experience navigating symphonic prog territory, while Kalle's heavy guitar solo propels the band to musical Olympus. Antony elevates each musician, drawing out their very best. "Beyond the Mirror" features a saxophone attack that remains firmly rooted in the 80s, with vocals from Per, who has just released a top album with his band. A duet with Antony and the female choir recounts the finality of life. Beyond the conventional melodic and melancholic feel, Marek's saxophone returns for the symphonic finale, leading into the exhilaratingly catchy "How Fragile We Are," perfect for sinking deep into your armchair. Olha's ethereal vocals over Antony's keyboards, their sweetness escalating to candy cane, the tempo slowing, the vocals narrated, Kalle's slide guitar and the saxophone simply reinforcing this intimate atmosphere with Pascal's Chapman guitar. "The Glass of Time Part 2" follows, closing the album; Antony and his organ-like keyboards let the notes rise. A reprise of Part 1 with more flavor, initially reminiscent of Vangelis; The bucolic air glides over the OLFIELD countryside before culminating in an ethereal mood, enhanced by the guitar of another prodigy, Michel. The finale is Genesis-esque, bringing the album full circle and demonstrating the intense prog structure it establishes.The only downside is that it's no longer KARFAGEN musically speaking, but it's excellent. (4.5)KARFAGEN successfully follows up OMNI by incorporating different talents onto the vocals of this conceptual sequel. Powerful lyrics, a striking prog cover, melodies that invite you on a journey, and prestigious guests. OMNI, interesting when I myself refer to it as an unidentified musical object in my annual lists, is a symphonic rock opera concept album that forms the continuation of this cycle. OMNI is for immersing yourself, traveling, and dreaming.The only downside is that it's no longer KARFAGEN in fact, but it's excellent.

items.body: Review by alainPP — DEVIN TOWNSEND, his 23rd album after more than 40 years of innovation, is a rock opera born from 10 years of collaboration with the Noord Nederlands Orkest symphony orchestra. His line, "Courage is not the absence of fear, it is being truly afraid and facing it anyway," demonstrates his unwavering determination.A solemn opening, like a semi-prologue, soaring and orchestral, with the voice as the creative foundation; mysterious pads on war, an epic, trumpets, and the music begins. An instrumental opera above all, the soaring voice, the instruments shifting from gentle to titanic, in true TOWNSEND fashion. We enter the city and the thoughts of a man grappling with his questions.'Covered by Causes' is a climactic attack, the instruments tuning up, a Floydian Wallian note, and the wall of the orchestra begins to move, languid and dramatic. It's ever-changing, electro-dub at times, vibrant, mysterious, majestic, and oriental, like 'The Mothers'. 'Orion' has a wild sound, with its goose-like croaking; a piece lasting over an hour with a stunning, spacey 'Intermission'.'Lexin Returns' returns with mysterious voices, a typical preparation for war, reminiscent of Carmina Burana, the mocking heavy riff kicking off 'The Big Snit'. The finale, starting with 'A Life', strikes me as more expressive, modern, avant-garde, in fact. 'Metamorphosis' extends this fantasy-opera-classical-Townsenian universe, riding the wave of power from the symphonic orchestration imbued with rock sounds. The theatrical moment of delving into Devin's mind as if into the skin of John Malkovich? 'Stained Hearts' features Anneke singing, her phrasing instantly recognizable before the aggressive, then ambient, finale, the duality so dear to Devin making its mark right to the end.Devin Townsend created this chrysalis-like opera with the help of Steve Vai, his friend since 1993, with Anneke van Giersbergen as the other guest vocalist. Devin wrote everything, taking his time?10 years in fact?to realize his childhood dream, aided by the conductor of the Noord Nederlands Orkest. An album as a testament to his faith in music, a long, sincere album composed of three distinct parts.(3.75)

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — 'Systematic Chaos' is studio album number nine from Dream Theater, released in the summer of 2007through Roadrunner, the band's debut on the label. This album comes right after the massive liverelease 'Score' (2006) and the excellent preceding studio album 'Octavarium' (2005). Featuringseveral long and complex pieces, this is one of the lengthiest and perhaps most demanding DT albumsfrom the 2000s, exhibiting a really aggressive, ballsy sound, somewhat similar to their 2003 release'Train of Thought'. To me, 'Systematic Chaos' is all about that cutting-edge technical display,which is intertwined with some truly frantic sections, as this album definitely features some of theheaviest Dream Theater recordings ever. Stylistically, there is very little separating this albumfrom the couple of studio LPs that came before it - the compositions are epic and complex, the musicis theatrical and aggressive, and the instrumental fireworks display is all over the place on SC.Kicking off the album we have 'In the Presence of Enemies', the longest album track that is split intwo parts that bookmark the record. The band did not want to open or close the album with a twenty-minutes-plus song, which is why the song was split in two. Many of its sections offer the typicalDream Theater sound, which we recognize as sharp and bombastic, often featuring excellent melodiesand blistering riffs. Petrucci's contribution to this piece is particularly impressive and theinstrumental passages are absolutely astonishing. Part I of the suite is followed by 'Forsaken', amore straightforward song that introduces a melodramatic sound that might not please all thelisteners (me included). We then have the three middle tracks, which for me represent the strongestpart of the album - both 'Constant Motion' and 'The Dark Eternal Night' bolster a riff-heavy,muscular modern metal sound, while the darker atmosphere of 'Repentance' is peculiar but moving,which is a bit uncommon for a DT album. The 15-minute-long suite 'The Ministry of Lost Souls' is atechnically-proficient epic that never stuck with me, unfortunately, and the song 'Prophets of War'sounds rather bland compared to the rest of the album. However, closing off 'Systematic Chaos', wehave the second part of the 'In the Presence of Enemies', which is effective and aggressive,capturing several peak performances from all five band members.Overall, this record follows the familiar, tried and tested, prog metal formula from the band'sprevious albums, which for me strips 'Systematic Chaos' of originality. Nevertheless, the quality ofthe music is exceptional, and this album features some of the heaviest and crunchiest Dream Theatermusic released to date. Furthermore, James LaBrie sounds very confident and mature on this album,displaying some of his strongest vocals ever.

items.body: Review by kev rowland — Back in the glory days of vinyl, buying a record was not just about the music it contained but what came with it. There would generally be wonderful artwork, possibly lyrics, maybe even a gatefold sleeve, but some artists took it even further. Being a keen Jethro Tull collector I revelled in the programme which came with 'A Passion Play' and the pop-up figures on the sleeve for 'Stand Up', but of course the highlight was the mighty 'Thick As A Brick'. Not only was it musically their finest hour, but it also came inside a broadsheet newspaper which even included a review of the album itself! I spent many hours reading this, as I am sure many other fans did as well, but with the advent of CDs and digital downloads this style of presentation mostly disappeared. I thoroughly enjoyed the release of 'Mad Martins' by Gary Miller back in 2018 which brought a highly researched 100-page book to the table, and now we have Tom de Wit, who surely must have brought himself close to the edge of insanity with this project.His last release was 2023 with Dreamwalker's Inc. and the concept album 'The First Tragedy of Klahera' and it would have been easy for him to follow with more of the same, but instead he decided to immerse himself in a very different project indeed. Why not create an audio drama show on YouTube (season 1 is already released and season 2 is following later this year), record a soundtrack containing 73 tracks (virtually all instrumental, nearly 3 hours long), deliver an 80-page artbook containing the story which is released with it, plus a videogame (in development) which builds on the same? Tom provides lead vocals, backing vocals, rhythm guitars, percussion, keyboards and orchestral arrangements and his brought in others to help him achieve his vision, including guitarist Lennert Kemper who has been working with him for more than a decade, plus others on harp, bass, drums, sax, flute, koto, violin, viola and cello as well as plenty of singers for the choir. The use of real instruments instead of keyboards has had a huge impact on music which for the most part is modern orchestral mixing in with prog metal.Of course, while playing the album, one needs to be reading the incredible artbook which comes with it which explains the stories behind all the characters as well as providing artwork which depicts them all. There are art and descriptions accompanying every song, all 73 of them, and then at the end of the book are photos and information about everyone involved. One completes it all, then starts to wonder what is next? A proper book is surely not out of the question, filling in all the missing pieces and providing the details we have not come across yet, and what about a full-length feature cartoon? Possibly the largest achievement with this album is that I thoroughly enjoyed playing it even without all of the visual cues which come with it, and that is quite something when it is 3 hours long, covers a multitude of musical styles but is often orchestral, with little in the way of vocals. It is a massive piece of work, and although the album has now been released there is still a lot more to come before this chapter is complete, and one can only wonder if Tom is still sane enough to travel this road again in the future or if he will take a very different path altogether. He has never been one to do what is expected of him and continues to surprise.Available as a triple CD (or on USB, which is not something one sees often), this is actually an album deserving of a quadruple vinyl release, and it is a shame I cannot see that happening due to cost but there is no doubt this is a release which in many ways defies description yet is thoroughly enjoyable throughout and is definitely something to which I will often be returning. If you want the complete aural and visual adventure, then this is one to seek out.

items.body: Review by KansasForEver4 — It took fourteen years for L'OMBRA DELLA SERA to follow up their self-titled album released in 2012, which at the time was a side project of LA MASCHERA DI CERA, both under the guidance of Fabio ZUFFANTI. Here, he is joined by the cream of the crop of Italian progressive music: Alessandro CORVAGLIA (keyboards and vocals), Agostino MACOR (keyboardist and cover designer), the excellent drummer Andrea ORLANDO, and the equally excellent saxophonist/flautist Martin GRICE.This "Segreti nel Nero" is conceived as a film, or more precisely, as a filmed symphony, composed of ten tracks. Eight of these tracks run between 3:35 and 6:43, while two others are epics, as they say in the world of progressive music, where vintage instrumentation takes center stage. Some tracks are complete reinterpretations of pieces from their first album, which may displease many music lovers. The opening track, "Albert e L'uomo Nero," sets the overall mood of the album, swirling and swirling, driven by Martin Grice's wind instruments (8/10)."Gamma," gentler in its opening, illuminated by synthesizers, with a generous dose of mellotron in its second half, is near sublime, Italian progressive rock (IPR) at its finest (10/10). It's a shorter version of the opening track from their 2012 debut album, with a killer sound. "Portrait of a Veiled Woman" is a simple, tranquil interlude, primarily driven by Martin GRICE (7/10), which serves as an introduction to "Fantastic Fly," the first piece presented to the media. It was an excellent choice, given its striking formal beauty (9/10). The majestic keyboards and the rhythm section (Fabio ZUFFANTI and Andrea ORLANDO) create a hazy, ethereal soundscape, while Martin GRICE's saxophone playing is non-stop."A Come Andromeda" is propelled by bass guitar and deep, dark keyboards before a flute-like refrain (again by Martin) that lasts until 3:36. This leads into a rather surprising jazzy interlude, a bit of a jarring departure in my opinion (7/10). It sounds more like a big band performance, perhaps in the vein of EWF or CTA, to stay closer to the progressive rock genre. "La Traccia Verde," which follows with a lively, almost danceable rhythm, showcases Agostino Macor's Fender piano before a vibrant organ solo, all illuminated by the magnificent saxophone of Maestro Grice (8/10). "La Ballata Di Carini" is one of the album's vocal pieces; Alessandro Corvaglia had to contribute, after all. It's a theatrical piece that didn't really convince me (7/10).We now come to the main course of the album, "Le Venti Giornate di Torino" (The Windy Days in Turin), a nineteen-minute epic that Robert Fripp's band, from the "Islands" era or even "Starless and Bible Black," wouldn't have disowned. It features numerous flute variations and trills, Alessandro's soothing voice (I prefer him when he's not straining it), and a martial rhythm from the eleventh minute onward, dominated by the rhythm duo (9/10), before the explosion, the final whirlwind that leaves us in a state of intense bliss. "Canto Campane" offers a gentle interlude with flute, piano, and Andrea's pads, a welcome respite from the previous track. It's true RPI in the classical vein, good but nothing more (7/10).Let's close the album with "A Blue Shadow," the second epic track on the record. A somber piano, a gentle saxophone, the majestic mellotron orchestrating the whole, then, from the fourth minute onward, the rumbling bass of Fabio Zuffanti, the abundant percussion of Andrea Orlando, and the frenetic saxophone, all lead us into a mysterious maelstrom. Once again, it's very Crimson-esque in spirit and execution (9/10), and the finale is breathtakingly beautiful.A rich work, not easy to grasp, which will require multiple listens for all music lovers.Originally published at profilprog.com

items.body: Review by KansasForEver4 — The Italian band WISH has existed since 1992, but their first album (which I haven't heard) wasn't released until 2019. Here we have their second album, released in late spring 2026, recorded by the same musicians.This album is the fruit of a long journey. Its writing began in 2019, a few weeks after the release of their first album, "Stay Here My Friends," like a necessary exhumation of the past. The current dramatic and unpredictable global situation has brought us back to the stories told in this album.Its title, "The Endless Winter," is clear: WISH speaks of war as an endless winter, gray, desolate, and as dark as can be, pushing back all hope of a bright future. WISH followed in the footsteps of the missing, visited the D-Day landing sites in Normandy, and gathered testimonies for a timeless yet very real concept. This album is dedicated to all those who witnessed the horrors of that not-so-distant era.August 6, 1944, a date forever etched in history for France and its allies. "Pointe du Hoc," the instrumental that opens WISH's album, is a little gem (I don't usually comment on tracks shorter than three minutes). It features the ebb and flow of the sea, the drone of planes overhead, and the soaring flute solo of guest Susanna Felicetti for a theme that truly moves you (10/10).A near-perfect transition to the album's longest track, "Comandante Nino" (10/10), clocking in at eleven minutes. Welcome to Piergiorgio Franceschelli, whose English accent is more than respectable for an Italian vocalist. The flute once again works wonders, and Giorgio Simonetti on six-string is no slouch either; a great lyricism emanates from his instrument, both electric and acoustic. "Collapsing" is more guitar-driven, with Salvatore Patti's keyboards more understated. The fretless bass, played by another guest, Graziano Brufani, takes center stage. This track leans towards hard rock or progressive metal, keeping things current (8/10)."The Four Rooms" (9/10) is brilliant symphonic progressive rock, though not necessarily original. It's easy to listen to, beautifully sung by Piergiorgio, with Graziano's fretless bass laying down an impeccable sonic backdrop, before a lovely Moog solo by Salvatore at 4:58 (unfortunately too brief at barely thirty seconds).The transition to "I Watch You from Afar," of almost the same length, begins with an ethereal piano, again featuring the fretless bass (things come in threes), and Salvatore Patti's synthesizers shine over Massimo Mercurio's drums before a six-string solo ignites the piece midway through. Piergiorgio's vocal phrasing sounds distinctly world-weary while remaining pleasant (9/10).I don't usually dwell on tracks shorter than three minutes (which doesn't mean I don't listen to them), but WISH will be the exception. "On The Trail," an instrumental composed by Salvatore, is illuminated by Susanna Felicetti's flute. Let's move directly to the closing track, "This Life" (9/10), the one chosen by the band to introduce the album. This six-minute piece summarizes the narrative WISH intended. A very calm track, like a softened Roger Waters (the melancholic side), it again features Susanna and her flutes and concludes with a very lyrical guitar solo.Without bias, I wasn't expecting the Roman quartet to reach this level, which makes it a very pleasant surprise, as the story being told is a significant element in my appreciation.

items.body: Review by The Progolyte — This will be the last jazz rock/fusion album from Italy I will be reviewing as I come close to the end of my deep dive into Rock Progressivo Italiano and its various forms. It's a relatively obscure one-off project named Bella Band their self-titled debut record contains a mere half-hour of music to go into. Listening to it, it's your run-of-the-mill jazz fusion album of the seventies, having those fun and quirky vibes on similar bands from the country like Arti E Mestieri, just maybe a little less technical and highly skilled. The members of the band play alright, but I've definitely heard better across the hundreds of jazz albums that I've listened to. With all that being said, it's still a charming little project that can display the elements of jazz fusion and its characteristics. The personnel includes Riccardo Cioni on keyboards, Roberto Buoni on woodwind and brass instruments, Luigi Fiorentino on guitar, Mauro Sarti on bass, and Tonino Camiscioni on drums to cap it off. The songs here are all quite short, being between five and ten minutes of length. They're all pretty good and well-put-together pieces, if a little uninspired at points. For the most part, while it does have its highlights, a lot of the album seems to lack an identity or something that makes it unique and has it stand out among the dozens of other small jazz fusion records that came from Europe in the late seventies. One of the things I did like about it, though, was that it was more in touch with earlier fusion instead of the more funk and accessible direction the genre had seemed to be taking at that moment in time. Going forward, side one was my favorite of the two sides, having the longest track, Promenade, as well as my favorite one, Fairadiesis, which was a high energy and engaging composition reminiscent of Jean Luc Ponty or Mahavishnu Orchestra. Overall, while it could use some extra details, I think the band did a good job with what they recorded, and it was a nice experience in the moment. In conclusion, I think I'll be sticking with a low 3.5/5 or high 3.25/5 for Bella Band's one and only album. It just doesn't kick as hard as I was hoping, and there feels like something is missing from it. If they had that one spark of creativity and originality that I love in all of my favorite albums, then maybe I would've given it a higher score.

items.body: Review by The Progolyte — My introduction to the more modern Rock Progressivo Italiano band, Nuova Era, was their most recent studio record, 20,000 Leghe Sotto I Mari, which came out last year and is apparently both their second best and second most rated album. The reason it lays behind the first place spot is the band's 1995 project, Il Passo Del Soldato. This is, according to ProgArchives, one of the best Italian albums of the time period and the best to come from the nineties in the country. With all this acclaim surrounding it, I knew I just had to check it out. After my first few listens, this is quite a strong album, combining elements of older Italian albums like Terra In Bocca, Darwin, and Zarathustra with a more polished (almost neo-prog) twist. There's a ton of grandeur surrounding the music, as well as being drenched in tons of symphonic keyboards that echo back the amount of different sets Keith Emerson would play on. And while the songs on here are all quite short (most not even breaking eight minutes), there's still a lot of material packed into these pieces. The album is very consistent in terms of musical quality but seems to get lost when it comes to keeping things fresh. Sure, the music here is very strong at points but can feel a little forgettable as it doesn't advance in the ways I was hoping for. Beyond that, there's not really much to criticize here. My favorite composition was Lo Spettro dell'Agonia sul Campo, which is around seven and a half minutes of mostly instrumental music that can get that bombastic symphonic sound found in the Scandinavian bands while still having that lighter tone to it. My other favorites include the title track and Armicrazia, which were the longest and most detailed pieces on the record. I also really enjoyed the more antique and medieval feel of the material, with the various melodies giving off a very interesting, classical, and engaging tone to the songs. At parts it can feel a little soulless, but it's all around very strong and full of interesting elements to be picked apart. In conclusion, I had a lot of fun with this one, and though the hype didn't fully translate when I listened to it, I would say this is still worth checking out if you want to get into the modern Rock Progressivo Italiano scene, as it is one of the first of its kind. I'll be rewarding this one a strong 4/5.

items.body: Review by kev rowland — To celebrate their 20th anniversary, Canadian outfit Versa have combined the two parts of their 'A Voyage/A Destination' albums which were released in 2022 and 2024 respectively and combined them into one lengthy release (3 hours) with additional tracks/ performances. The first thing I noticed, even before putting it on the player, is that the cover of the new collection is virtually identical to that of Part Two, which seems very strange to me. This is the first time I have come across this band and albums, so I was intrigued to hear what they were like, especially as the press release says how highly they were regarded within the prog scene. I also noticed a huge number of guests, including Jim Grey and Sam Vallen of Caligula's Horse, Nick D'Virgilio (Big Big Train), Marjana Semkina (iamthemorning), Eric Gillette (Neal Morse Band, Temic), Ross Jennings (Haken), Lars Fredrik Fr�islie (Wobbler), Kelly Nordstrom (eMolecule, Sound of Contact) and Michael Trew (Moon Letters) which can often bode well (Semkina in particular is hugely under-rated).There is no doubt this is a very clever album with a large amount of instrumentation and orchestration, and multi-instrumentalist and composer Matthew Dolmage has obviously spent a great deal of time on the arrangements but I soon found that listening to this was more of a chore than a pleasure, and it just went downhill for me from there. The combination of post rock and progressive rock is intriguing, and individually the performances are excellent but there was little here for me to grab onto and when I started looking to see how much longer there was until it ended I knew my view was not going to be the same as those who have lauded these albums very highly indeed. Somewhat interestingly, they were entered onto ProgArchives in October 2024, but since then there have been zero reviews of their first three albums and only one for 'Part Two', so does that say something about how widely they are known or about the albums themselves? Discuss.I have nothing against lengthy albums or songs, but with nothing here connecting with me either musically or lyrically all I can say is this is not for me. I am sure those who enjoyed the albums when they were originally released will gain a great deal from this expanded release, but I cannot imagine it is something to which I will ever return.

items.body: Earlier Belgian electro-industrial project Suicide Commando released “Come Down With Me (V2025)“. The track previewed “Collective Suicide Vol. 1+2”, an anniversary release out now, June 5, 2026. The earlier released EP also included “Jesus Freak (Die In Agony)”, “Death Lies Waiting (Death Will Find You Remix)” and the new track “Control & Consent”. Suicide Commando now marks the 40th anniversary live during 2026. Confirmed dates include a São Paulo show at VIP Station on August 22, 2026. “Come Down With Me” was originally released on “Implements Of Hell” in 2010. “Collective Suicide Vol. 2” is out as digital, CD, double vinyl and as part of the limited “Collective Suicide Vol.1-2” wooden fan box set (limited to 200 copies). The box includes the “Collective Suicide Vol. 2” digipak CD, yellow 2LP, red 2LP of “Collective Suicide Vol. 1”, a 36-page photo book and a hand-numbered certificate. “Collective Suicide Vol. 1” was first issued for the project’s 30th anniversary in 2016 and now receives a vinyl edition for the 40th anniversary. The collection covers recordings from 1987 through 2016, while “Collective Suicide Vol. 2” focuses on later material, rare tracks and reworked versions. Below is the vinyl tracklist. “Collective Suicide Vol. 1” tracklist Side A: “Suicide”, “Industrial Underground”, “Incinerate”. Side B: “T.V. Obsession”, “Come To Me”, “Kevorkian”. Side C: “Disposable Paradise”, “Body Count Proceed (2007 Re_Count)”, “Hate Me”. Side D: “Until We Die (Single Edit)”, “Body Machine Body (Demo Version)”, “My New Christ”. “Collective Suicide Vol. 2” tracklist Side A: “Infliction Of Pain”, “Severed Head”, “Come Down With Me (2025 Version)”. Side B: “Kill All Humanity (Short And Painless)”, “Evacuate”, “Unterwelt (Apocalypse)”. Side C: “Control & Consent”, “Fate (Death is coming…again!)”, “Face Of Death (2023 Mix)”. Side D: “Death Lies Waiting (Death Will Find You Remix)”, “Jesus Freak (Die In Agony)”, “Better Off Dead”. About Suicide Commando Suicide Commando is the electro-industrial project of Belgian musician Johan Van Roy. The project started in Leopoldsburg, Belgium, in 1986. Van Roy began experimenting with electronic music in 1986 and released his first tape under the Suicide Commando name two years later. He bought a Roland SH-101 in summer 1986 and then added Boss DR-110 and Boss DR-220E drum machines. He also named The Cure, Sisters Of Mercy, Depeche Mode, Fad Gadget, The Neon Judgement, Front 242 and The Klinik as early influences. Before the 1994 debut album “Critical Stage”, Suicide Commando released a run of cassette material, including “Suicide Commando”, “This Is Hate”, “Industrial Rape I”, “Crap”, “Go to Hell”, “Into the Grave”, “Industrial Rape II”, “Black Flowers” and “Electro Convulsion Therapy”. “Critical Stage” was released on Off Beat and was followed by “Stored Images” in 1995 and “Construct-Destruct” in 1998. The later releases includes “Mindstrip” in 2000, “Axis of Evil” in 2003, “Bind, Torture, Kill” in 2006, “Implements Of Hell” in 2010, “When Evil Speaks” in 2013, “Forest of the Impaled” in 2017 and “Goddestruktor” in 2022.

items.body: The German EBM and electro act Digital Factor will release the album “0.8” on June 12, 2026 through the Belgian label Alfa Matrix. The twelve-track record arrives on CD (pre-order is available via Alfa Matrix), and in digital formats. It follows the band’s 2021 album “A Chemical Process” and the 2023 charity album “G.B.A. – General Behavior Abrogate“. The band now is a duo with Mike Langer and permanent new member Gwendolyn Gaffa who already contributed on the EP “They Will Forget You (When You Die)” and on the 2023 charity single “I Am What I Am“, released as a free download. ‘0.8’ tracklist, guests and 1980s concept The album contains twelve tracks and two guest features. Franziska Haucke appears on “Never”, and Marie-Luis Kiessling features on “We Are Blind”. The record is a return to the band’s formative era, diving deep into the musical and cultural DNA of the 1980s. The first single “They Will Forget You (When You Die)” for instance already carries a nod to Depeche Mode’s “People Are People”, while the album track “Time” is presented as a homage to Kraftwerk. Langer also used a special production method for “0.8”. He deliberately stepped away from modern production perfection, using stripped-down setups and monophonic synths to recreate the raw textures and subtle imperfections of early electronic music. Good to know, “Feel To Little” uses speech fragments from Charlie Chaplin films, while “Never” is set to a James Bond-style atmosphere. 0.8 by DIGITAL FACTOR About Digital Factor The band formed in 1993 in Altenburg, Germany. The founding lineup consisted of Torsten Heise, Mike Langer and Tino Schmidt. The project first brought a mix of EBM and electro, later adding techno, synth-pop and crossover elements,. They played early live support for acts such as Placebo Effect and X Marks the Pedwalk. The band’s first release was the 1994 EP “F.A.L.L.I.N.G.- Down” on Hard Records. A move to Hyperium and Hypnobeat followed, bringing the debut album “Relationchips” in 1995 and the conceptual second album “On Demand” in 1996. Tino Schmidt left the band in its earlier years, and in 2010 Torsten Heise left and was replaced by Leo von Leibnitz. Come With Me EP by DIGITAL FACTOR The album “A Chemical Process” arrived in 2021, alongside remastered reissues of the back catalogue. The EP “What?” followed in 2022, and 2023 brought the charity single “I Am What I Am“, the “Ouvre” EP and the charity album “G.B.A. – General Behavior Abrogate“.
